opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the pieces are closer than people assume, but there are a few specific bottlenecks that matter more than raw scale.

The first is reliability over long horizons. Current models can do impressive things in a single turn: write a function, sketch a proof, summarize a paper. Research isn't a single turn, though. It's weeks of trying an idea, watching it fail, figuring out *why* it failed, and deciding whether to push harder or abandon it. If your per-step error rate is even a few percent, it compounds badly over hundreds of steps. So a lot of what's needed is error correction: the ability to notice "this result looks wrong," go check it, and recover without a human stepping in.

The second is what I'd call research taste. Knowing which problems are worth working on, which experiments will actually be informative, and when a surprising result is a bug versus a discovery. Humans build that through years of feedback. Models get some of it from pretraining on papers, but papers are a heavily filtered, post-hoc story. They don't show the hundred dead ends. So you probably need training signal from actually running experiments in environments where outcomes are verifiable, something like RL on real research workflows rather than imitation of finished artifacts.

Third, memory and continual learning. A human researcher accumulates context: they remember that this dataset has a weird labeling issue, that this optimizer was finicky last time. Models today mostly start fresh or rely on stuffing things into a context window. Some form of persistent, updatable knowledge seems pretty important.

And then there's the less glamorous stuff: tool use, running code on clusters, managing compute budgets, reading logs. A lot of ML research is engineering, and I suspect that part gets automated first, and it'll accelerate everything else.

The reason I care about this, from a safety perspective, is that automating AI research is plausibly the point where things can move very fast. If you have thousands of copies of a competent researcher running in parallel, the pace of progress could jump in a way that outstrips our ability to evaluate and govern it. So I think we should be measuring these capabilities carefully, with benchmarks that actually track autonomous research ability rather than trivia, and we should have thresholds and safeguards defined *before* we get there, not after.

r002.rationale: It discusses models, pretraining, and RL, but does not predict that the system would be built almost entirely with deep learning.

r003.rationale: It calls for persistent, updatable memory of research context, but does not connect that memory to inheriting culturally accumulated knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer this as the guest, in Dan Hendrycks's voice, without using tools.

Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we're probably not as far as people's intuitions suggest, but the bottlenecks aren't where people usually point. The thing people fixate on is raw intelligence, like can the model solve hard math problems, can it score well on benchmarks. And I spend a lot of time on benchmarks, so I'll say that's necessary but it's really not the hard part anymore. The models are already quite capable at the sort of local reasoning that goes into research.

What a human-level AI researcher actually needs, I'd break into maybe three or four things. The first is long-horizon agency. Research isn't a question-and-answer task, it's months of work where you form a hypothesis, run an experiment, it fails for some dumb reason, you debug it, you realize your hypothesis was wrong, you revise. Current systems degrade badly as the horizon stretches out. They lose the thread, they don't maintain a coherent model of what they've tried and why. So you need something like persistent working memory and the ability to recover from errors over thousands of steps, not just tens.

The second is taste. A lot of what distinguishes a good researcher from a mediocre one is knowing which problems are worth working on and which directions are dead ends before you spend six months on them. That's a very hard thing to get from pretraining, because the data you'd need is mostly in people's heads, not written down. I think you partly get this through reinforcement learning on actual research outcomes, where the model proposes experiments and gets signal on whether they panned out, but that's slow and expensive and the reward is extremely sparse.

Third is the compute and infrastructure side, which is unglamorous but it matters. An AI researcher has to actually run experiments, which means orchestrating GPUs, dealing with flaky clusters, managing data pipelines. You want a model that can do that reliably, and reliability is a different axis from capability. A system that's brilliant ninety-five percent of the time and catastrophically wrong five percent of the time is not something you can let run unsupervised for a week.

And then fourth, I'd say there's a scientific-method piece around calibration and self-skepticism. Humans are bad at this too, but a good researcher knows when a result is too good to be true, checks for leakage, looks for the bug that would explain the surprising number. Models right now are a bit too willing to accept a result that confirms what they were hoping for. That's partly a training-incentive issue.

So what does it take technically? I think it's mostly scaling plus a lot of RL on agentic, long-horizon tasks with verifiable outcomes, plus better scaffolding for memory and tool use. I don't think it requires some new paradigm. That's actually what worries me somewhat, because if it's mostly an engineering problem, it's the kind of thing that could happen faster than our institutions are prepared for. Once you have systems that can do AI research at human level, you have a recursive loop, and the speed at which that compounds is really the thing I'd want people paying attention to. That's why I think of it less as a pure capabilities milestone and more as a threshold where the governance questions stop being hypothetical.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between a system that can answer questions about machine learning and a system that can actually do research. For the latter, you need something that can close the loop: identify a useful problem, form a hypothesis, design an experiment, write the code, interpret the results, and revise its approach when it turns out to be wrong.

A lot of the difficulty is in deciding what to work on. You can generate plenty of plausible ideas, but which ones are worth spending a month testing? That requires judgment about what’s tractable, what would be informative, and what would matter if it worked. And then you need enough reliability to carry a project through many steps without a small mistake derailing everything.

I don’t think we know whether that requires some fundamentally new architecture. It could be that stronger models, combined with tools, persistent memory, and training on extended research tasks, get us much of the way there. But I’d want to assess that through actual research outcomes. Can the system independently produce a result that survives scrutiny, and can it do that repeatedly across unfamiliar problems? That’s a much stronger test than being able to propose an impressive-sounding research direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is getting systems that can do long-horizon research, where you don’t already know what the answer should look like. That’s a different problem from answering a question that somebody can immediately grade.

An AI researcher needs to identify a useful problem, form hypotheses, run experiments, notice when the results undermine its assumptions, and decide what to try next. Current systems can help with individual parts of that process, but reliably putting the whole loop together is much harder. If you make a small mistake at every step, that compounds over a long research project.

Technically, I’d expect you’d need stronger reasoning, good access to computational tools, and some way of learning from experiments rather than just producing plausible explanations. You also need evaluation environments where making genuine scientific progress is rewarded. Otherwise, you can end up training something that’s very good at writing papers that sound convincing.

I’m uncertain whether that requires a fundamentally new architecture. It could be that scaling existing methods, combined with better training on extended tasks, gets us much of the way there. But I wouldn’t equate doing well on a collection of difficult questions with being able to autonomously do research. Choosing the right questions and following through when the feedback is ambiguous are a large part of the job.
